Mr. Speaker, I want today to pay tribute to Mrs. Guylaine Saucier, an exceptional businesswoman who has just been elected President of the Quebec Chamber of Commerce. I wish to emphasize that it is the first time in the whole history of that organization that a woman is appointed to that position. For the past eleven years, Mrs. Saucier has been Chief Executive Officer of Les produits forestiers Saucier Ltee, a major sawmill firm in Abitibi. She is a very active and dynamic woman who can serve as a model for people in Abitibi-Temiscamingue and the rest of Canada. Her corporation is at the forefront of modern technology, with a constantly increasing turnover which amounts to $7 5 million today.
Mr. Speaker, the Lebel-sur-Quevillon Chamber of Commerce, through Lucien Vallee, its President, the mayor, Denis Levesque, the Lebel-sur-Quevillon and Comtois residents and I have organized a party last Saturday to fete Mrs. Saucier and express to her our admiration and that of all Abitibi men an women.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) that, according to the information I have, the announcement last Monday of the criteria for the Laprade Fund has failed to quell the dissatisfaction prevailing in the Conservative Party's regional caucus on that issue. Indeed, many questions remain unanswered, and this was recognized even by some Conservative Members. I share that view,
inasmuch as we are entitled to ask why such a long delay in coming up with those general requirements, that could have been announced a long time ago.
Could it be that the dice are loaded in favour of some of the projects, so that monies already would be earmarked for the opening of an aluminum wheel plant in the Louiseville area? As it happens, Mr. Speaker, Louiseville is in the constituency of the President of the Treasury Board.
I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, and I know the Conservative Members also are concerned with the distribution of the Laprade Fund. How will the President of the Treasury Board proceed in order to honour his previous commitment to ensure a fair and just distribution in the areas concerned? The criteria for eligibility to the Fund are one thing, but criteria for a just and fair distribution of funds are quite another.
I have nothing against the Laprade Fund being used to build a plant in Louiseville, but it is my view that all projects should be processed, examined and announced simultaneously.
I serve notice to the Speaker and the President of the Treasury Board that I will be acting as a watch-dog on that issue.

Mr. Speaker, the Forget Report was tabled only a few days ago and I would like to bring to the attention of the House one of the recommendations in the report, that is Recommendation No. 36.
Mr. Speaker, the Forget Commission recommends that the Governement establish the new Unemployment Insurance Commission as a parent Crown corporation, set up under Part II of Schedule C of the Financial Administration Act.
Do you know what that means, Mr. Speaker? The Forget Commission is recommending that we turn the Unemployment Insurance Commission into yet another Crown Corporation. Mr. Speaker, the Canada Post Corporation situation is reason enough not to make the same mistake twice.
A Crown Corporation is a parallel power, a sort of second power within the state-over which the Government loses control and to which it no longer can give instructions for its good performance.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to strongly oppose that recommendation. We have no need for another inefficient monster like the Canada Post Corporation-let us not create another one with the Unemployment Insurance Commission.

December 11, 1986

subsubtopic: TELEVISING OF FILM TOMMY DOUGLAS-KEEPER OF THE FLAME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight is a special night for most Canadians, particularly New Democrats. At eight p.m. CBC television will air the NFB film Tommy Douglas-Keeper of the Flame. Directed by Elise Swerhone, the film is about Tommy and his work on behalf of all Canadians, particularly the little guy. Thousands of Canadians will be gathered around their TVs tonight to watch the story about their hero, the little fellow who brought them medicare. Unfortunately, not all CBC stations are carrying the show this evening. According to the agreements between CBC and its affiliates, this is not one of the shows which must be carried by the affiliates.
Local TV stations in at least two communities have decided not to air the show tonight. In Thunder Bay and London viewers will be able to watch an American TV program, Sidekicks, instead of a real Canadian show with a real Canadian hero, Tommy Douglas. I urge viewers in London, Thunder Bay, and any other city where the show will not be aired to call their local CBC station and cast a vote in favour of Canadian history, and get them to air Tommy Douglas- Keeper of the Flame.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY'S NEED FOR ACCESS TO UNITED STATES MARKET
CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY'S NEED FOR ACCESS TO UNITED STATES MARKET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House will be pleased to learn of the full endorsement by Canada's shipbuilding industry of our Government's intention to negotiate a comprehensive trade agreement with the United States. I recognize and sympathize with the difficulties facing shipyards and shipyard workers across the country, difficulties which would be greatly eased on the West Coast by the early award for the construction of the Polar Class 8 ice-breaker to British Columbia. However, the increasingly assiduous implementation of U.S. restrictions such as the Jones Act and the Burns-Tollefson amendment which prohibit or obstruct Canada's access to the U.S. marine market for construction and repair work are having a negative impact on all Canadian shipyards.
Changes are needed, such as the extension of the Canada-U.S.A. Defence Production Sharing Understanding to include naval vessels. I share the opinion of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association that such changes under a new Canada-U.S. trade agreement would be of significant economic benefit to the shipbuilding and allied industries of both
countries, and would strengthen the North American defence industrial strategic base.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL PAROLE BOARD-RELEASE OF CONVICTED MURDERER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a federal inquiry is necessary into the hideous first-degree rape and murder of 21-year old Celia Ruygrok by an individual who was on parole for a previous gruesome murder. It has raised disturbing questions about our parole system and the operations of the halfway house where the murder occurred. Supreme Court Justice David Watt said: "Logic and reason were obviously not applied" in releasing the murderer on parole.
The parole system has failed in a very fundamental way. The system must assume some responsibility for the Ruygrok murder. How and why was the murderer released after serving only nine years of a life sentence for the original murder? The bottom line is that he should not have been released. The National Parole Board must account. If Canadians are to have confidence in our criminal justice system, a full and complete inquiry is necessary into this miscarriage of justice. Mr. Speaker, I call on the Government to order an inquiry at the earliest opportunity.

Yesterday in the House, Mr. Speaker, the former Solicitor General of Canada and present Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) stated that the Quebec Association of St. John Baptiste Societies is an extremist group.
This is the kind of arrogance which, so prevalent in the Liberal Government of the 1970s of which he was a member, had then given rise to serious social upheavals in Quebec and even led to loss of lives.
The Liberal Member, speaking from his seat in the House as a prestigious former Minister, made a vile attack against the St. John Baptiste Society.
Mr. Speaker, my grandfather owes to the St. John Baptiste Society the fact that his grandson can now speak French in the House. It ranks among the leading defenders and outstanding proponents of the development of French culture in North

America. As a Member from Quebec I cannot accept attacks against this group of francophones.
Mr. Speaker, the statement of the former Liberal Minister is insulting and, made as it was in the absence of the accused, comes from a petty coward.

subsubtopic: COMPANION OF THE ORDER OF CANADA-THE HONOURABLE JOSEPH ROBERTS SMALLWOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to rise and pay tribute today to a great Canadian, the little fellow from Gambo, Joseph Roberts Smallwood, otherwise known across the country as Joey, who is today receiving our country's highest honour, Companion of the Order of Canada. Due to his ill health, he is receiving it in St. John's from the Lieutenant Governor, the Hon. James McGrath.
Journalist, broadcaster, labour organizer, farmer, politician, statesman, and the only living Father of Confederation- without him we would not be a province of this country today. His legacy of bringing Newfoundland into Confederation and bringing the advancements to our province which we have seen over 23 years with him as Premier are adequate testimonial to him.
However, I want to pay tribute to him today. I am sure the House would want to join me in expressing that. We in Newfoundland are proud to be Canadians. There is no one prouder today than Joey Smallwood. I am sure Members on both sides would want to join me in offering our congratulations and best wishes to him.

Mr. Speaker, one could not ask for a better time to comment on this Government's plans, both present and future, for privatization than after the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) made the Freudian slip of referring to Air Canada when he should have said Canadair. That is further evidence of what the Government has in mind concerning privatization. It is more than what we have seen so far with de Havilland and Canadair.
As a Member of Parliament from Winnipeg I have a particular interest in the sale of Canadair to Bombardier. Many Winnipegers believe for good reason, and I share that
belief, that the recent award of the CF-18 maintenance contract to Bombardier instead of Bristol Aerospace in Winnipeg had its genesis in the sale we are now debating which this Bill implements. If there was ever unanimity about anything in Winnipeg, there is unanimity in the anger over the awarding of that contract. The bid by Bristol was technically and financially superior. In the minds of Winnipegers there is unanimous distaste for this purchase of a Crown corporation by a private company, precisely because we believe it may go as far back as when this deal was originally struck, that the Government may have made promises to Bombardier that it would receive the CF-18 contract in return for going ahead with the purchase of Canadair. If that is true, and there is no way to absolutely prove it, and it is ever found out to be absolutely and undisputedly true, then one of the greatest political frauds ever will have been perpetrated on the City of Winnipeg and Bristol Aerospace. They would therefore have been led through the whole bidding and tendering process when the decision may well have been already made at the time the deal this legislation implements was made.
What is it in particular that angered Winnipegers about the CF-18 contract? I want to say for the benefit of Conservatives in the House that I think one of things was that it went against every single principle ever uttered by the Progressive Conservative Party up until its election in 1984. Who more than Progressive Conservative Members stood in this House time and time again to criticize Liberal Governments for making decisions on political grounds rather than on sound business grounds? We can still hear the echoes in this Chamber of Conservative MP after Conservative MP criticizing the Liberal Governments for doing that. Yet what happened with the CF-18 contract? Exactly the same thing. I can understand why the business community is so upset, particularly with the Progressive Conservative Government, because Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament gave them reason to expect that business criteria and business criteria alone would be used to determine who got the contract. I do not say that business criteria should be the only criteria for the awarding of contracts. Yet the Progressive Conservatives did and consistently so. Therefore, when the CF-18 contract was awarded on a different basis, you can understand the confusion, dismay and sense of betrayal felt by the business community, western Canadians, and particularly Winnipegers. They had every reason to believe that if the tendering process was allowed to take its natural course the contract would go to Winnipeg.
The awarding of that contract to Canadair goes against everything the Government has ever said about the way in which to deal with foreign businesses. This corporation was a good foreign corporate citizen. As far as I know, it had reinvested all its profits in the industry in Winnipeg. The Progressive Conservative Government made a career in opposition of criticizing the Liberal Government for the way it dealt with foreign corporations. Good corporate citizens are hard to come by. When you find one you should regard it as a
December 11, 1986

rare thing. Bristol Aerospace reinvested in Canada rather than sending its profits back home. The Progressive Conservative Government awarded the contract on political grounds, going against everything it had ever said about the way in which Governments ought to award contracts.
Many Winnipegers believe that Canadair should have remained in the public sector. However, whether Winnipegers are on the right or the left, whether they think privatization is good or bad, we all agree that if there was a hidden understanding at the time of the sale of Canadair to Bombardier, and if part of it was that the CF-18 contract would go to Bombardier, then that would be a very serious and offensive fraud perpetrated against the people of Manitoba.
I would like to say a bit about privatization. What does the Government think it is up to when privatizing Crown corporations? Does the Government believe it was a sound business move to privatize the corporations which it has? I find mysterious the intensely ideological core which seems to be behind these privatization measures.
Crown corporations cannot win with a Progressive Conservative Government. If they are losing money, that is a sign that they are a burden on the public Treasury, that Government cannot manage a peanut stand, and that Government should not be involved in things which should more properly be left to the private sector which, according to Conservative mythology, can do everything so much better than the public sector. In fact, half the Crown corporations exist because Governments moved in to save the remains of an industry which had been wrecked by the private sector.
However, let not the facts confuse Conservative mythology with respect to privatization. If a Crown corporation is losing money, that is all the more reason it should not exist. If a Crown corporation is making money, that is all the more reason for it to be in the private sector because things which are profitable should be kept in the private sector.
It seems to me that according to Conservative policy there are no circumstances in which public ownership is preferred. When a Crown corporation is losing money, it should be in the private sector. When a Crown corporation is making money, it should be in the private sector because we cannot have Governments making money. There is no circumstance in which it would be all right to have a Crown corporation.
The only conclusion which we can reach is that the root of the Conservative drive toward privatization of Crown corporations is ideological. It has nothing to do with whether a corporation is losing or making money, whether it is providing a good service for cost, whether it contributes to regional development, or whether it serves some other useful public purpose. None of that has anything to do with it in the final analysis.
The Government has developed a hit list of Crown corporations which it would like to privatize. We do not know exactly what is on that list. We do not know which corporations are the Government's favourite, but perhaps the Deputy Prime
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
Minister gave us a hint today when he said "Air Canada" instead of "Canadair". Perhaps that is some indication of what the Government has in mind for us next.
There are other approaches. If people are unhappy with the way in which Crown corporations are run, there are solutions other than privatization. Simply to categorize the situation which we now face as either pursuing the status quo, which is basically a status quo developed by Liberal management of Crown corporations, or privatization, is to restrict severely the choices available. That severely narrows the range of options with regard to how Crown corporations may operate more efficiently, be more sensitive to the needs of the economy, and be more profitable. There are alternatives to selling these Crown corporations at fire sale prices after the public has invested hundreds of millions of dollars, as in the case of Canadair, in a major economic sector.
The people of Canada invested hundreds of millions of dollars in the aerospace industry, and that investment paid off. During the 1970s and early 1980s there were huge losses as a result of a depression in world aircraft markets, but Canadair became profitable a couple of years ago. In 1985, it recorded a $20 million profit and had great expectations for the future. Is that the time to privatize a Crown corporation? According to the Conservative philosophy that Crown corporations should be privatized whenever you can privatize them, it would be. It does not matter to Conservatives whether Canadair was making money, but it matters to us. Not only has the Government divested itself of a profit-making Crown corporation in a very important industrial, technological and economic sector of the Canadian economy, it did so at the same time as the investment made by the people of Canada in that company came to fruition.
Is it a sound business principle to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in a corporation and, just when your investment is going to reap some benefit, sell it for next to nothing to someone who will not be accountable to the goals you set for that industry when you made your investment? Does that make any sense unless you have a blind ideological commitment to privatization regardless of the consequences?
I suggest that that is exactly what happened. The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) is known as one of the ideological zealots on the Conservative side of the House. He wanted to sacrifice a few Crown corporations. Hopefully it will be only a few. Hopefully we will not see the wholesale kind of privatization which has taken place in Great Britain, for instance, as a result of the commitment of Conservative Parties to privatization.

I just hope the Government has the good

I mentioned earlier that I thought there were different ways of getting at things which have irritated, not just the Government but other Canadians about the way in which corporations are run. A lot of it has to do with accountability and the feeling that Crown corporations become entities unto themselves. They become governments unto themselves in some cases and simply do whatever they like. The best example of that is AECL. It does whatever it likes whenever it likes. It goes through a lot of motions, but those motions are all set up by the Atomic Energy Control Board which is part of the same club. As far as I am concerned, if there was ever a bad example of public ownership-although I am not sure I would want to have it in the private sector-it is Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. It is not accountable and exhibits all the worst behaviour of Crown corporations.
The key is not to privatize, but to make Crown corporations more accountable, more democratic, more participatory, and bring more people into the decision-making process, particularly in important economic sectors. They should be more responsive to the needs of communities, to the rights of individuals and to the over-all economic health of the country. These are the kinds of things that people who are not seeking simple solutions might be thinking about. Instead, the Government takes a simplistic view that we should take important areas of our economy and turn the future of those important areas over to corporations which do not necessarily make decisions in the national interest, particularly when it comes to multinational corporations, although in this case it is a Canadian-owned corporation. The sale of de Havilland to Boeing would be an example.
The Government is turning important areas of our economy over to decision makers who have the publicly stated goal in life of making as much money as they can, whether they do it in the market-place or by squeezing grants and loans from the Government-farming the Government system, so to speak, in whatever way they can to add to their particular profits. Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of comments and then perhaps a question for the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). First, the Hon. Member attempted in his dissertation to try to tie the sale to Bombardier of Canadair with the CF-18 maintenance contract. The Hon. Member also alluded to the decision of the Government to privatize. I want to bring to his attention that the Budget in May 1985 outlined the basic principles of the Government in carrying out privatization initiatives. The principles are; first, to be sensitive to the concerns of management and employees of corporations when we have considered candidates for sale; second, to consider the impact of privatization on consumers and the market competition; third, to consult with provincial Governments; fourth, to avoid selling at distress prices for the sake of privatization; fifth, to follow commercial objectives when considering the stages of privatization where there may be periods of mixed, private and public ownership; and sixth, to examine all related policy and financial considerations on a case-by-case basis before considering privatization of any given corporation.
Several benefits are expected as a result of returning federal corporate holdings to the private sector. Privatization will reduce the size of government and leave room for more private sector initiatives and will promote market competition and more efficient allocation of resources. It will improve company efficiency through market discipline and by reducing political and bureaucratic impediments. In some cases, privatization may encourage individual Canadians to take part in the ownership of major corporations through equity investments.

I thought it interesting that the Hon. Member referred to the objectives of privatization as outlined by his own Government and mentioned the objective that Crown corporations not be sold at distress prices merely to transfer them quickly to the private sector. What could be more distressing than this deal? Bombardier is paying $120 million less than the $300 million liquidation value, the $224 million book value, and the $300 million to $400 million estimated technology value. In addition, it will receive $50 million in federal grants in January with $30 million to come, unspecified export financing, a $1.7 billion CF-18 defence contract, no financial obligation relating to Canadair's debt or outstanding liabilities, plus profits of $20 million in 1985 and $2.8 million in the first quarter of 1986. That is not bad for $120 million and the equivalent of $20 million in royalty payments. That is what I call a distress sale. It is what I call doing something for ideological purposes only and for no other good reason.

Mr. Speaker, I always listen to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) with interest and with benefit. Today I was especially interested in the logic he directed against the Government saying that, the Government feels on the one hand, if Crown corporations are losing money they should be sold, and on the other, if they are making money they should be sold. He accuses us of having a blind ideological commitment.
I want to say that the same logic applied to the argument of the Hon. Member shows that if there is a blind ideological commitment in the House it is one which he and his Party represent. Their reasoning with respect to Crown corporations is precisely as he has described, namely, if a Crown corporation is losing money it demonstrates to the NDP that we need that Crown corporation. In their eyes it demonstrates that it is a public service that cannot finance itself through private efforts and therefore the good money of the taxpayers has to be poured into it. On the other hand, if a Crown corporation is making money then according to the NDP that shows that socialism works. It shows that we need more and more such Crown corporations in the eyes of the Hon. Member and his Party. The blind ideological commitment is across the way. Members opposite want nothing but a blind commitment to use more and more of the taxpayers' money and effort to keep alive Crown corporations, an effort that thus far the people of Canada have not entrusted them to expand.
I wish to point to a questionnaire I circulated in my constituency asking for public opinion on whether or not certain Crown corporations should be privatized. In all but one instance the respondents favoured the privatization of the named Crown corporations. So when the Hon. member speaks about the Government showing good sense, the good sense of the public as I ascertain it is that we want Crown corporations to be privatized as far as possible. Crown corporations should be continued only when there is an overwhelming and obvious reason to justify their continued existence. It is on that
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
pragmatic basis that Conservative Governments have been prepared either to organize or to continue Crown corporations.
The Hon. Member mentioned the CNR. It was a Conservative Government in the 1920s that put the CNR together, when there was a pragmatic need which justified it. When the time comes for a pragmatic value to privatize, then a Government should be prepared to take that step.

Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a view expressed by Members opposite that somehow when we privatize that the taxpayers do not have to pay any more. Yet I just went into a long description which no one disputed about the ways in which the taxpayers have already paid. With respect to what they have already paid, they will not be able to reap the benefits in terms of the investment they have made. Whatever money is made in the future by Canadair, now that it is in a profitable position, will not go to the taxpayers of Canada. On the face of it, it seems to me that this deal goes against the financial interests of the taxpayers of Canada. It is not something that should be regarded with relief by the taxpayers.
With respect to the so-called blind ideological commitment, the best that I can offer is an example that goes exactly contrary to what the Hon. Member was talking about. The NDP Government in Manitoba recently privatized a Crown corporation, Flyer Industries Ltd. The Government felt that, all things considered, this was the best thing to do in terms of the future of that particular industry in Manitoba, and for all the other reasons that may have entered into it. The Hon. Member is caught out on the facts on this one because there is an NDP Government privatizing a Crown corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my colleague a couple of questions. Since we socialists have to teach Conservatives about sound business practice, 1 would like to ask my colleague if he agrees that the taxpayer as an investor through his or her Government is not entitled to the same opportunity to receive a return on that investment as is a private investor. In terms of sound business practice is it not true that when a business is sold the buying company buys the accounts receivable and the accounts payable? In this case is it not so that Bombardier is buying the accounts receivable but the taxpayers are allowed to keep the $1.2 billion in accounts payable? What kind of sound business practice is that?

Mr. Speaker, it is not a sound business practice at all. However, it is very characteristic of the type of deals made between Government and the private sector when Crown corporations are being privatized. It is very typical of the type of thing that goes on. It is the taxpayers, the very people whom Hon. Members opposite say they are so concerned about, who get dinged in this kind of process. They are the ones who get to pay without any return on their investment. It is the private sector that gets the fire sale price for the technology of the future. The future of the industry is dumped into its laps for next to nothing. It is the private sector that will reap the profits and not the Canadian people.

speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) who will be the last Member to have 20 minutes in which to make his speech.

Thank goodness, Mr. Speaker. I thank Hon. Members for this chance to enter the debate on this important issue.
If it were not for Crown corporations I suspect that this country would still be so many acres of uninhabited snow. Throughout the history of the country we have seen a tremendous role played by Crown corporations. It was a Crown corporation which developed the intercontinental railway from Ottawa to the East. Crown corporations gave us broadcasting when in its absence we would have been entirely dominated by the United States and its broadcasting system. We saw Crown corporations give us air service at a time when this country would have been left with no option but to be the further extension northward of U.S. services. Crown corporations have been an important line of defence in the protection of Canadian nationalistic concerns against the pressures of the very much stronger, very much more dynamic economy to the south.
That is the backdrop to this debate. Of course, it is not a justification for keeping Canadair in the public sector. To Keep Canadair in the public sector would require a careful analysis of the potential benefit of its contribution to an industrial vision for Canada. Unfortunately, the Government has given us no such industrial vision for the future. Its vision is clouded. It is unannunciated. If anything, it is a vision of somehow surviving, somehow thriving by tying ourselves to the United States with a free trade agreement. We must deal with the question of Canadair not in the way we should, that is, as part of the development of an industrial base in Canada. Instead, we have to deal with it as a commercial transaction.

I must say, Mr. Speaker, that this is like a commercial transaction. There would be terrible losses here for any Canadian who pays taxes.
Mr. Speaker, I can give you figures that confirm what I am saying. First, I would like to point out that the Canadian public has invested $2.2 billion in this company! Based on the figures, we also know that the book value of company assets amounts to $478 million. Mr. Speaker, we therefore have a company which has received a lot of money from the Canadian public and which still has a lot of money left.
What price should Canadians pay for all that, Mr. Speaker? I must say that the price is terrible, shocking! It is a price that has nothing in common with the level of costs on the basis of Government statistics which may be found in the comparisons, in the financial aspects of the Bombardier proposal and if we look at the total we see it is less than $160 million.
Mr. Speaker, it is not fair to sell a corporation when there is so much difference between the costs incurred by Canadian
taxpayers and the price paid by the private company for that same corporation. It is not fair.
[DOT]	(1550)

It is for that particular reason that we find ourselves so strongly opposed to this transaction. We are not opposed to it because it is the sale of a public company. That is an important part of it but, as we have indicated, there are certainly cases of public companies being sold to the private sector and there are cases of private-sector companies brought into the public sector. However, to initiate a commercial transaction that is somehow equitable is not the same as to initiate a commercial transaction that results in the Canadian taxpayers getting hosed and ending up with far less of a return than they should be getting. This is something that is not acceptable from a commercial perspective. It would appear only to be justifiable for, as my colleagues have pointed out, ideological reasons.

It is for an ideological reason. It is for reasons that make no sense that this corporation is to be sold at such a low price. We cannot approve of that transaction.

It is also important to note that this company is not some kind of a basket case. It is not a company that is dealing with its future prospects with a grim certainty of facing yet more losses. Again, according to the Government's documents, the net profit of Canadair was $6 million in 1984. In 1985 it was $15.2 million, and in 1986 the forecast profit according to the CDIC plan is $23.8 million. I predict that this case will be exactly the same as the case of de Havilland. After the company was sold the profits started to mount, profits which should have gone to the Canadian taxpayers who financed the incredible investments in the new technology which is now of such benefit to the owners of the company.
In addition to these points, we note again that this transaction is not normal. Again, I refer to government material from Salomon Brothers. Salomon Brothers is not exactly part of the socialist hordes, at least according to its latest membership list. It is clearly indicated within this document that the letter of intent includes provisions which do not conform to commercial norms. In view of the low price and the need to justify this sale, I would have expected Conservative Members to put before us a case for the sale of Canadair. I have not heard that case. All I have heard is that it is a fine thing to transfer things to the private sector. If that is not ideology, I do not know what is.
[DOT]	(1600)
A pragmatic, economic view would surely offer us some justification for this transaction, and that has not taken any precedence in this debate. That is our view. We are not committed to public ownership or to private ownership. As I have stressed in the past, we are committed to improving our
December 11, 1986

position in Canada in the face of very difficult challenges in the years ahead. These challenges will face us in the aerospace industry, the auto industry, and in virtually any industrial sector noted across the board.
We must stop using ideology as the response. It is ideological for me to stand up and say a solution to the automobile problem which looms before us is to nationalize all of the Canadian auto companies. That would be nonsense. It would certainly not be what we would expect to carry out in Government.
If there is a case in this instance for a transfer to the private sector, let us hear it. We have not heard it. We expect that we will hear it during the hearings that we anticipate will take place on this Bill. As in the case of deHavilland, we hope that there will be witnesses called to indicate to us what was contained within their bids, and whether they might have been superior to this ridiculously low bid we have received here. We expect that these hearings will take some time to put the case clearly before us. When these hearings do take place, I hope that it will be possible for those who support this sale to indicate quite clearly why it is that this private transaction to the private sector should be supported. If that evidence is brought before us, I am sure that we will be quite open to argument. So far we have not had that position put forward, and we can only take the ludicrously low price as the basis of our opposition to this sell-out of an important Canadian resource.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions and comments, the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James).

I would like to make a rebuttal to the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). In the first place the Hon. Member talked about Salomon Brothers and, certainly not being part of their establishment, I believe that he was referring to their August 11, 1986 letter that talked of non-conformity to traditional commercial practice. The Hon. Member did not read the whole paragraph, and I would like to set the record straight. Salomon Brothers stated:
The only important provision in the LOI that neither promotes Crown objectives nor conforms to traditional commercial practise is that which provides for risk sharing should insurance become "economically impracticable to procure".
As the Hon. Member knows, that was in connection with the serious problems that we have today with liability insurance.
I am sure the Hon. Member also has the letter of June 24, 1986, which is a letter from Marsh & McLennan in relation to this subject. The letter states in connection with Bombardier Inc. that:
They have agreed to purchase insurance without any participation of premiums by the government. In the event the insurance may not be available they propose to share the cost of the claims with the government for a 15 year period on a sliding scale.
The letter further states:
It is obvious from the foregoing that the Bombardier proposal is clearly superior in that it relieves the government of any on-going premium involvement or financial participation in deductibles. We feel there will always be insurance
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
available in some form and therefore the proposals made by Bombardier and CAT in the event insurance becomes unavailable are academic.
In addition, I wish to speak to some other comments made by the Hon. Member of the opposition. Earlier he said that deHavilland would in essence go down the tubes, that it would not be successful. Now he says that it is successful. That certainly gives no credit to private enterprise to that end.
In 1982 and 1983 Canadair lost $1.2 billion primarily due to many write-offs. By the end of 1984 the Crown investment in Canadair had reached $2.2 billion. A comment was made earlier by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) when he was talking about the financial side of this transaction. He failed to mention in connection with that sale that the federal Government has some caveats.
The commitments that are made by Bombardier will be encouraged by the Government through retention of special shares which can only be earned by Bombardier if they deliver on the commitments in R and D, and so on, as the Hon. Member knows well. Additionally, the Government retains the rights to the Challenger technology, therefore preserving the investment of Canadians in this technology over the years.
In many ways, Canadair's technology is now being put together with a skilled workforce, and members of that very same skilled workforce are writing to this Party today and to all of us stating the importance of this sale to Bombardier. So we have Canadair's technology teamed up with a skilled workforce in the Province of Quebec. All of us know that it is very important to the province to make a successful private sector company that will carry on with this very important work.

Within that range of words, as I identified them, I think there were four points. The first point was with respect to the Salomon Brothers' comments. I wish to quote from the letter of intent:
The LOI also has within it a number of provisions that do not conform to commercial norms. Most (though not all) of these operate directly or indirectly to promote Crown policy objectives. Examples include a provision to preclude land speculation, mechanisms to encourage employment, growth, reinvestment and retention of sufficient working capital and an undertaking not to relocate material facilities outside of Quebec.
So certainly, there were factors other than the insurance factor that were noted within the letter.
Second, the comment of Marsh & McLennan about insurance being available, and again I quote from the Salomon Brothers' letter:
-if insurance becomes unobtainable at economically practicable cost.
That "-at economically practicable cost" clearly can leave much more risk than the Member has implied.
I have a third point in respect of the special shares and the guaranteed royalties. The suggestion of the Hon. Member was that these somehow raised dramatically the price for Bombardier. I had already included them within the price I noted in

December 11, 1986
Adjournment Debate
my discussion. According to available government documents, the special shares are worth, at most, $10 million. The guaranteed value of royalties is worth, at most, $20 million. When added to the $ 120 million cash on closing, the dividend, and the payment for the airport, the total value received by Canadian taxpayers will be well under $160 million for a company with assets of $470 million, according to the August 19, 1986 edition of The Globe and Mail. I suppose one for three is not a giveaway in some people's books. However, it looks like a gross transfer to the private sector. As I said before in a previous speech, it is another gift-wrapped present for Christmas to private enterprise from the Tory Government.

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) liberate himself from the ideological incarceration of the previous NDP speaker. It is clear from the very fine speech made that the basis for this consideration should be pragmatic objectives. I should like to dwell for a few moments on that point.
As is very often the case in the sale of a Crown corporation, it is not always possible for a Government to achieve the kind of sale which each of us would like. This was the problem facing the Government of Manitoba when it sold the Flyer bus line. As was reported in the Winnipeg Free Press, it would have been cheaper to close down the company than to enter into the sale, as did that Government. The sale was undertaken after the Government tried for years to cope with a failing Crown corporation, and it ultimately cost the taxpayers of that province $96 million. It would have been cheaper for that NDP Government to close down the company.
Very often a Government cannot obtain the kind of sale its critics and its opposition would recommend. However, there are two gains to the public by the sale of a Crown corporation, as in the case of Bombardier and as in the case of de Havil-land, which I think need to be noted. The first is that the burden is taken off the backs of taxpayers. Year after year taxpayers' moneys were poured into the corporation to cover losses and to subsidize the company. That will finally be brought to a close. Second, by putting the company into the hands of more efficient and effective salespersons and managers, job security is given to the personnel which they lacked beforehand. When representatives are called before the parliamentary committee, the numbers should include the workers in the company who will now have job security.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for being the first I have heard in the debate to address the question of the very poor price received for the company. Frankly, his position has proved the point I was making. In the case of Flyer Industries, it was the takeover of a bus company which was losing money. It was a question of whether it made sense to keep pouring money down that sink-hole. The answer seemed to be no, that it made more sense to privatize it.
In the case of Canadair, we are talking about a company which has made profits for the last two years, and the projection for the coming year is that it will make even greater
profits. Therefore, the choice before them was not to sell the company or face losses; it was to sell the company or keep the company. The company was finally providing to taxpayers the kind of return it should have provided all the time, had it not been for mismanagement under a previous Government.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-25, an Act to authorize the divestiture of Canadair Limited and to provide for other matters in connection therewith, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment (Mr. Benjamin)(p.l866).

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join in the debate on the privatization of Canadair. It is a significant event in the political and aeronautics history in Canada, although it is not an event about which I am happy.
Years ago when the Government of the day made a policy decision that the aerospace industry must be protected, it was clear that Canadair could not be allowed to go out of existence. At that time it was important for us as a nation that it be retained, and the only way to retain it was by having its assets owned by the Government of Canada, mainly because the private sector failed to ensure its viability. Whether it was through its products, marketing, or whatever, I do not know. It was up to the Government of Canada and the people of Canada to sustain that operation. Sustain it they did for a number of years. Millions of dollars were poured into the industry. I do not have to ask the workers to know that they would rather have real jobs and the money coming to them in
December 11, 1986

that way than being on unemployment insurance or welfare. We must recognize that while it was referred to as a drain, it was an investment in human beings. It ensured that the industry survived and that the workers had paycheques with which to look after their families in an appropriate Canadian way. It was not a drain; it was an investment in the future.
Now the Government has decided, as part of its ideology, to get out of the business and to give it away to the private sector. Let us take a look at what Bombardier is getting for its $120 million. It is getting a company with a Canadian book value of $224 million, a technology value in the neighbourhood of $300 million to $400 million, and a liquidation value of around $300 million. It is quite clearly getting a good deal. It is almost as good a deal as the one given by the Ontario Liberal Government this week to the Four Seasons hotel chain. For a nominal sum of $4 million to sell Minaki Lodge, the private sector picked up $11 million in tax deductions. In effect taxpayers paid to give away that lodge. It is almost the same situation with Bombardier. It is getting much more than the value of the amount to be transferred.
I should like to refer to one aspect of that value. It is my understanding that three Challenger jets are currently grounded in West Germany. They have been grounded since February. They are grounded because Canadair was unable to supply the maintenance manuals in a properly translated form to be used by the German workers. Because of that grounding and because Canadair has been unable to live up to its responsibilities, the West German Government is withholding $60 million owed to Canadair. Where does that $60 million show up, Mr. Speaker? Will that $60 million be paid to Bombardier, and does that actually reduce its cost from $120 million to $60 million? Is it getting an even better deal than we think? Is that money showing up elsewhere? Will it come back to the Government of Canada? Who will be receiving that money? Those are the kinds of questions that should be answered in this House to ensure that Canadians know what kind of a deal their Conservative Government has arranged for them.
We also have to recognize that Canadian taxpayers get to keep Canadair's $1.2 billion long-term debt. I thought when one company bought another company it was a package deal. You got the receivables on one hand but you got the other side of the ledger as well. You get the bad with the good. Clearly, Bombardier is taking only the good. It has not taken the overall responsibilities. Canadian taxpayers will never get that money back. They will not get a return on their investment. It was their investment, not the Government's investment in that company many years ago. Canadair was just beginning to show a return on that investment. I believe that for the last year for which we have information a profit of $20 million was made, a small amount compared to the $1.2 billion of long term debt, but it was a start. That money could have been used to help to pay for other worthwhile projects in Canada,
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
projects paid for by the Government of Canada. I think the Government is wrong in deciding to privatize this company.
I can understand, as others have said, that if you have a situation where a company owned by the Government has a questionable value that requires massive amounts of money on an ongoing basis with no return, there would be a need to wind it down to see if somebody in the private sector would be willing to take it over. I come back to Minaki Lodge in Ontario. Taxpayers paid $50 million for that. One million a year is still being paid out to operate it. Minaki Lodge should never have been owned by the Government of Ontario. It had no business being in that kind of a situation. Ironically, it was Ontario's Conservative Government that nationalized Minaki Lodge and nationalized Cancar Rail in Thunder Bay, but a Liberal Government sold them. Here we had federal Governments nationalizing industry and Conservative Governments selling them. It just proves once again that there is no real difference between the Liberals and Conservatives in this country when they change hands, federally or provincially.
Those are my few contributions to the debate. Perhaps the Hon. House Leader in his business question today was giving us advance notice of yet another attempt to privatize something when he referred to this Bill as the privatization of Air Canada.

PROVISION OF LOW COST LOANS TO FOOD PRODUCERS Mr. Nelson A. Riis (Kamloops-Shuswap) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of establishing an Agribond program that would provide for low-cost loans to hard pressed Canadian food producers.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to present this motion to the House today. I am hopeful that Members of Parliament will in good Christmas spirit support the consideration of it. After all, it simply asks Members to put on record the fact that we are committed to the concept of the family farm. It asks Members to say that we want to see the family farm continue as a viable food-producing unit in Canada.
This motion is but one option in terms of providing longterm low interest funding for family farms and family ranches.
Basically, it is an appeal to members of the Government to stand up and say that the Government of Canada is 100 per cent committed to the family farm and the family ranch and that it is not about to cave in to the pressures of agri-business or corporate agriculture.
I need not go into the details of the virtual pending crisis facing our farm community. Something in the neighbourhood of 40,000 farms face critical financial crisis, and many more are experiencing serious financial difficulties. The situation worsens by the month. I know that in my constituency of Kamloops-Shuswap on a drive through any traditionally productive agricultural valley today the most predominant feature on the landscape is the for-sale sign. As a matter of fact, some of the valley drives have become known as drives through "Billboard Alley" because of the huge signs setting out lands for sale and various financial arrangements that can be arranged and so on. It is a very serious situation. It exists in all parts of the country and has been recognized to a certain extent by the recent government initiative to assist some of the hard-pressed grain producers. For virtually every single area of agriculture we could say that a similar situation exists.
In my own constituency, which I do not think is unlike most rural areas, we see, two or three generations later, the sons and daughters of those who cleared the land or broke the soil being forced off the land. In many cases they are being forced into seeking off-farm incomes. It is a very serious situation.
What the motion proposes is that as Members of Parliament we recognize that there are solutions to the very serious problems, the most critical of which is the debt equity ratio which our food producers face, as well as the massive capital costs which really prohibit young people from going into agriculture. We have an aging farm population. Our food producers are getting older and older and young people are not able to enter the profession. The average capital cost now for a farm or ranch is about $400,000, including land, equipment and building costs-to say nothing of the annual operating costs.
This is a very serious situation, one of the answers to which is the provision of a mechanism through which long-term low interest money can be obtained. Of course, the agri-bond concept is one which would allow that. Another solution which my Party has put forward on many occasions is with respect to parity pricing. In this situation what a farmer or rancher received for his goods would be a reflection of his costs. As a result of a parity pricing situation they would be able to maintain their operations.
Let us talk for a moment about agri-bonds. It is a concept that has received the support of all sides of the House as indicated in speeches by Members and their rhetoric over the years. It is an idea which was referred to the Finance Committee some months ago. In its final report the committee recommended that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) consider the advisability of establishing an agri-bond program and it set out some conditions. The first is with respect to eligible borrowers, which would include any farmer whose
December 11, 1986

equity is between 20 per cent and 50 per cent of assets. Such a program would be operated by the Farm Credit Corporation. A maximum of $300,000 per borrower would apply over the long term in terms of providing predictable interest rates.
Over the years many people have gone on record to say that they support this measure. On February 7, 1984, the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) had this to say:
Mr. Speaker, this motion is exactly the same as a motion presented by myself and 10 other Members of Parliament on November 24, 1983. The 10 were, the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), the Hon. Member for Cariboo- Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway), the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), the Hon. Member for Wetaskawin (Mr. Schellenberger), the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer), the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt), the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), and the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers).
In my seven years as a parliamentarian I remember hearing many Members of Parliament, both from the Conservative Party and from the Liberal Party, follow the lead of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), who time and time again has made the case for long-term low interest financing for farmers. He has suggested that some form of agri-bond would be an obvious course to follow.
In closing, I wish to say that if we were to support this motion it would help young people get into farming. It would allow prospective farmers and ranchers to develop themselves in these professions. It would help farmers who are presently experiencing a debt crisis and who have found themselves through no fault of their own in most cases in an impossible and increasing debt situation. Perhaps most important of all, it would provide a vehicle for investors to invest in agriculture. In this way people who want to buy or purchase an agri-bond would know that the money they are investing in the future of Canada is being invested in the future of agriculture in terms of the future of the family farm or the family ranch. It could even be tailored so that it could be invested in agriculture in the investor's part of the country. In this way people taking out agri-bonds would be able to say, yes, I have played my role. I have done what I could as an investor to put money into the hands of ranchers and farmers who are my neighbours or members of my own family. It is a tremendous vehicle.
The Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) indicated that both provincially and federally the Conservative Party supports the idea of agri-bonds. This is the acid test today. We will see whether all that has gone on before is mere rhetoric or in fact that members of the Conservative Party in this House actually support a vehicle which they have said on many occasions they support. It is a vehicle which would place low interest long-term money into the hands of our food producers and allow this matter to go to committee for further examination.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 5.02 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate initiated by my honourable colleague for
Agri-bond Program
Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) on the subject of agri-bonds. Of course, Mr. Speaker, my colleague has just suggested in his conclusion that it would be the true test if Conservative Members were to support his motion. I would like to tell that NDP Member that his party has always been making promises but has never had an opportunity to keep them, so making promises comes easy, and I would like to come back to this.
Mr. Speaker, everyone does recognize how urgent it is to deal with the matter of interest rates, and this is still more obvious to this Conservative Government because many of our Members also are farm producers. This means, Mr. Speaker, that certainly we need no advice from the New Democratic Party, and much less from the Liberal Party in order to know what we have to do to help farm producers across the land. It would seem, Mr. Speaker, that both Opposition parties, and especially the Liberals do not seem to understand that this Government, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) are not acting unilaterally but hand in hand with the provinces and farm groups to find adequate solutions to the problems that the farming industry is now facing.
Of course, we are not pretending that we know everything or that we have cure-all programs, as the Opposition parties are so prone to point out, and we are well aware of that. However, the progress made by this Progressive Conservative Government over the last two years where agriculture is concerned shows how much that industry is important to us and to all Canadian consumers.
Mr. Speaker, when we were elected in September 1984, the interest rate charged by the Farm Credit Corporation was 16 3/4 per cent; that was a shameful rate, and it was the clear, obvious and definite proof that the Liberal Government had knowingly abandoned agriculture, knowingly ignored the young farmers. Now that they are in Opposition, Mr. Speaker, they are urging us to make good the wrongs they did over the last 20 years. This is what the Minister of Agriculture, together with his provincial counterparts, obvious sectors of the economy and farmer's unions are doing, this is what we are doing as we showed once more this week by announcing a $1 billion assistance package for Canadian farmers.
Mr. Speaker, to give but one example of Liberal incompetence in the farming industry over their last mandate and the last 20 years, I would like to point out the crop losses caused in 1983 by drought in my own Province of Quebec.
The producers had experienced a crop loss. They sent an application to the federal Government-the Liberal Party was in power at the time-asking for help, but it was turned down. Mr. Michel Veillette, who was then the Liberal Member for the Champlain riding, followed his Government's recommendations. He said no, on the ground that Quebec was supposed to pay. But following our coming to power in September, 1984, Mr. Speaker, we have worked together with 1'Union des producteurs agricoles and our Minister of Agriculture to give back to Quebec producers the nearly $30 million to which they were entitled. We have compensated them for their crop losses, because the Progressive Conservative Government had made a

December 11, 1986
Agri-bond Program
firm commitment during the 1984 election campaign to help our farm producers.
That is a convincing argument, Mr. Speaker.
As I was saying a while ago, under a Liberal administration in 1983-84, the Farm Credit Corporation was lending money at 16 3/4 per cent interest. I should like to remind the Hon. Member who is laughing because her Government had lended money to farm producers at 16 3/4 per cent interest, that it is now lending at 10 3/4 per cent interest rate, and that was a commitment and is an achievement of this Progressive Conservative Government.
Thanks to these 10 3/4 per cent interest rates, Mr. Speaker, our producers are showing renewed confidence in the future and are working very hard to produce for Canadians food of the highest quality. I know that it is not enough, Mr. Speaker, and that we will have to continue working over the next two years with the Prime Minister, together with farm organizations and provincial Governments, in order once and for all to offer decent interest rates to farm producers generally. We have set up several mechanisms, even though Members of the Opposition seem to think that we have done nothing over the first two years- but we have set up several organizations to help farm producers facing financial difficulties! Let us not forget that, after we came to power in 1984, we renegotiated interest rates, which were at 16 3/4 per cent, to bring them down to 12 3/4 per cent. We set up Farm Debt Review Boards, Mr. Speaker, and implemented the 6 per cent policy for farms on the verge of bankruptcy. These are, Mr. Speaker, concrete evidence of what our Government has been doing. What more can you ask in two years? I would like to ask the Opposition, Liberals and New Democrats, that, instead of being against everything we propose, they help us adopt quickly policies which would allow our farmers to take advantage of reasonable interest rates. And we are doing just that, Mr. Speaker. Liberals, for example, cannot ask us to do in two years what they could not achieve in twenty. We have to catch up, Mr. Speaker, and that is what we are doing. With some cooperation from the two Opposition parties, if they would only agree to forget their partisanship and to work with us, as we are presently doing with farm organisations and provincial governments, we could, in a very short time, give farmers across Canada decent interest rates which would ensure that farming remains a major economic sector in our country.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 5.02 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to say a few words on the motion put before the House by the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) concerning agri-bonds. I think we just saw a beautiful demonstration of a Parliamentary Secretary for the Minister of Agriculture being totally rattled, into orbit, confused, distracted and on the defensive. I have never seen anything quite like it. It does not surprise me, because in looking at the record of the Government over the last two
years we can see why he is a bit nervous at the prospect of trying to defend the Government's position with regard to agribonds.
Of the 338 promises made by the Tory Party during the 1984 general election campaign let me refer to nine or 10 that have not been kept. Promise No. 3 was that the Tory Party would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to offer agri-bonds so that farmers could have access to reasonably priced funds. That promise was followed up in the spring of 1985, about three or four months after the Conservative Party came to power, with the unanimous report of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. That committee, composed of a majority of Conservative Members, recommended an agri-bond program. By that time in the fall of 1984 the farm debt crisis had been well catalogued by the Farm Credit Corporation. That committee report unanimously recommended that an agri-bond program with 8 per cent interest over a five-year term up to $300,000 per borrower be provided with the idea that it would be targeted toward people who were in serious financial difficulty allowing them to write down mortgages to 8 per cent whether they were with the FCC, or with other private institutional lenders.
I can certainly see why the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary was a little in orbit this afternoon, and very much on the defensive. If the rest of the promises are read, it will be seen that there are further recommendations that the Government would extend and expand the Farm Credit Corporation's special interest rates subsidy program, which of course they did not do.
Further on there was a commitment to allow the necessary funding to assist producers in refinancing their loans at current prevailing rates. Looking at the inventory of mortgages of the Farm Credit Corporation, 32 per cent of all the FCC loans were financed between 12.75 per cent to 16.75 per cent. Most of those 12.75 per cent mortgages were simply the $575 million conversion program of funds that were not used in the 1984-85 fiscal year of the Farm Credit Corporation to convert to mortgages over 14 per cent; not mortgages of 13, 13.5, 13.75, 14 per cent, but mortgages over 14 per cent down to 12.75 per cent. Those funds were in the FCC account and had either been borrowed from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, or from private markets which were in the FCC loan portfolio and were available to be loaned and were done at a conversion in that regard.
We looked through the Budget of 1985, and we have had the report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), but there has been no decision with regard to assistance for the farm debt crisis, even though 39,000 of our youngest, most productive, and most technologically advanced farmers were facing serious financial difficulties. Since that time, many of those farmers have gone into bankruptcy or have been foreclosed on. Even though there was a unanimous recommendation of the
December 11, 1986

Conservative members on the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, there was nothing in the Budget.
So we come around to the Budget of 1986 and, lo and behold, we see the commodity based mortgage which theoretically provides interest rates as low as 6 per cent, if the farmer has a low enough equity position in the farm. Many of the farmers will be financed at 7 and 8 per cent. But if we look at the Budget Papers, it is found that the write-down of those FCC mortgages provides only $20 million. Looking at what the provinces are doing, Alberta has a $2 billion program at 9 per cent; Saskatchewan has a $1 billion program of assistance at about 6 per cent. The Ontario Government has a program of some $50 million a year to assist in writing down interest to as low as 8 per cent.
But there are a few other catches in the commodity based mortgage. If the commodity value goes up, such as hogs have gone up by 25 per cent this year, and beef has gone up by 15 per cent, then the principal of the commodity based mortgage goes up. If that continues to rise, the individual who thought he was getting a mortgage at 6 or 8 per cent, or what he was eligible for as a result of the level of equity that he had in his property, ends up paying some 12.75 per cent at this time, or last spring it was 13.25 per cent. If he wishes to pay out the mortgage, he has to pay out the entire mortgage at that level.
On Budget night what looked like a program of $730 million over two years at 6 per cent, over the 10 year life of most of those mortgages turns out to mean that the individual will have to pay 12.75 or 13.75 per cent interest on those mortgages. If you do not have a FCC mortgage you are not eligible for any assistance. So the commodity based mortgage which looked great on Budget night has a number of adverse aspects to it, which certainly make it less attractive than programs of real support such as many of the provinces have adopted.
One other point I would like to make in the agri-bond debate is that a group of Members of Parliament went to Washington to look at its agri-bond and revenue bond programs in January of 1985. It was clearly found there that in the cost of the agri-bond system much of the benefit flows to the brokers, to the lawyers, and so on. We, on the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, came to the conclusion that if an agri-bond program is going to be provided, it should come from the FCC. The Government takes the money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, writes it down to what the concessional rate is at 8 or 9 per cent, and the interest paid on that becomes non-taxable if the principle which is very similar to the small business development bond is used. In that manner, it is targeted toward younger farmers who are not in a taxable position where the interest write-off is not so important, or to farmers in financial difficulty where, because of their financial position, the write-off is not so valuable.
The agri-bond idea is one which the Government has committed itself to. I hope that they will allow it to be reviewed by the committee, as the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) has suggested tonight.
Agri-bond Program

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to speak to this Bill today. Before I begin to outline some of the activities that this Government has been involved in, I realize the mover of this motion pointed out that we have a crisis in agriculture. Nobody on this side of the House would disagree with that statement. The Hon. Member also pointed out the initiatives that this Government has taken that have helped the agricultural sector.
I do have some difficulty with the comments of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), who should know better since he has been in touch with the agricultural community for many years. The Hon. Member spoke about the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture having his head in orbit. I would say to the Hon. I realize it is very difficult for the Official Opposition Member to speak kindly of the Government, especially considering that it did ignore agriculture for many years. Its advice to the farming community was, expand, expand; spend, spend. Get yourself into a great deal of debt and hopefully you will get out of it. That was the Government advice to the agricultural community for many years. Today, those same farmers who took the advice of the opposition Party when they were in power are the ones who today find themselves in the greatest difficulty.
One of the saddest things that we have to do as Members of Parliament is talk to young farmers who come into our offices looking for assistance. They always say they wish they had not taken the advice of the previous Government and borrowed and spent and got themselves into the position they are in today". The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) should hang his head in shame for the position in which his Government has put many young people in agriculture today. The Conservative Government is trying its best to help alleviate that situation.
I am pleased to outline some of the achievements of the Government. On the matter of the agri-bond program, as was pointed out previously by Hon. Members, the program went before a committee where its proposals were studied. One matter raised before the committee was why anyone would invest in an agri-bond program when he or she could obtain a better deal some place else. Farmers like everyone else will not invest in a program if they can go to the bank and obtain a better interest rate.
