speechtext:
Yes, in an agri-bond program slippage takes place, money is lost, and it requires the setting up of another bureaucracy. Why not do it with existing agencies such as the Farm Credit Corporation?
Some people may not realize just how big is the Canadian agricultural sector. Some 1.6 million Canadian jobs depend upon that sector. It is especially important to western and eastern Canada. Many rural towns especially depend upon the farm community for economic stability. In one way or other agriculture matters to all Canadians.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) pointed out Tuesday to the Outlook Conference, when farmers are hurting, the nation is hurting. The Government understands very well the importance of agriculture. We have demonstrated our commitment to the farm community with action. This is why we responded to the problems facing grain and oilseed farmers with a $1 billion assistance initiative, the Special Canadian Grains Program.
The Hon. Member for Algoma pointed out that there was nothing in the Budget for farmers. I point out to him that not everything has to be in the Budget. Over the next year $1 billion will be in the hands of farmers. The program is the largest single special program ever undertaken on behalf of Canadian farmers. However, it is not the Government's only agricultural initiative, far from it. Since the beginning we have placed agriculture at the top of our list. It was a priority at the last two conferences of First Ministers and in the Speech from the Throne. Agricultural initiatives introduced by the federal Government have contributed to the stability of the farm sector. Our actions have benefited western and eastern farmers-all farmers.
We introduced farm debt review boards. At least one board is operating in each province right now. They have the power to halt foreclosure actions against farmers for up to 120 days. This gives farm families the breathing space they need to negotiate alternatives to foreclosure with their creditors. The boards are in place to help them do that.
We introduced new and more flexible lending programs through the FCC. The commodity-based loan program has proven to be very popular with farmers. It now represents close to half of all new FCC lending. The shared risk program represents 13 per cent of all new lending under the Farm Credit Act. We committed $80 million to writing down rates over five years on about 5,600 high FCC loans.
We also introduced the Canadian Rural Transition Program which, for the first time, extends benefits to farm families that have reached the point where they are financially unable to
continue farming. So far three out of four applications, on average, are being approved.
We introduced a lifetime capital gains tax exemption of up to $500,000 on the sale of farm property. We introduced farm fuel tax rebates which will amount to a savings to farmers of about $160 million over two years. We are pushing harder than ever to sell Canadian grain, and we have met with success. This year we signed a new long term grain sales agreement with the Soviet Union, calling for the purchase of at least 25 million tonnes of Canadian grains. We reached a five year agreement for 2.5 million tonnes with Egypt. We also reached a three year grain deal with Brazil. Nowhere are these achievements on the international grains market more important than in western Canada where most of our grain is produced.
Finally, the approach of the Government has led to lower interest rates. Every one-point decline in interest rates represents an annual savings to the farm community of more than $100 million. Despite our many initiatives on behalf of farmers, we recognize that everything is not right yet. We intend to do more.
We believe that long term stability of the farm community depends upon Governments and farmers working together to plan the future. This is why the national agricultural strategy is so important. Every federal and provincial Minister of Agriculture has endorsed it. The strategy is our blueprint for the future. It is not a detailed plan of action. Rather, it is the framework within which Governments and farmers can work together.
The Government is certainly not ignoring the agricultural sector of Canada. We will continue to bring in programs to benefit farmers across the country, from the East to the West. They can count on us as a Conservative Government to do a good job for them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 5.02 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great pleasure to speak today on the motion concerning the agri-bond program presented by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of establishing an agribond program that would provide for low-cost loans to hard pressed Canadian food producers.
Essentially I agree and have agreed for some time that some system must be established to take the burden of debt, particularly high interest rates, off the backs of Canadian farm producers. However, I wonder how many Hon. Members remember that five years ago interest rates in Canada reached 22.75 per cent. Since that time we all know that they have come down.
During the debate today it was interesting to hear an Hon. Member opposite talk about commodity loans at 6 per cent, 7 per cent, and 9 per cent, and about some FCC loans presently being as low as 7.5 per cent and 8 per cent. This is not to say that the motion before us is not a good one. I think it is the
December 11, 1986

long term solution to a very difficult cyclical problem experienced by farmers. At times they may be doing well and commodity prices may be doing well. Then they are hit with drought, sometimes repeatedly, or a plague of grasshoppers. A number of such things can happen to them. Suddenly the benefit of the one good year is taken away by four or five bad years. There must be some way to improve the situation, and possibly an agri-bond program could do it.
Let us look at what has happened since the Government took office. Let us look at the trend and direction it has taken. I do this because I think the agri-bond issue is not the priority it was when interest rates were running from 18 per cent to 22 per cent. Although it still should be held high on the agenda and not put on the back burner, the emergency of four years or five years ago does not exist today.
Direct Government payments to producers have increased by more than fourfold, from $659 million in 1980 to an estimated $2.8 billion in 1986. To that $2.8 billion we can add another $1 billion for the 1986-87 fiscal year. One payment comes next spring, $300 million and $700 million. Direct Government payments have been particularly high since 1984. Let me repeat that. Direct Government payments have been particularly high to the farm community, the food producer, since 1984. In 1986, direct payments accounted for more than 10 per cent of total farm cash receipts of the average food producer in Canada. That is increasing and has increased since because of this last pay-out. That is a massive subsidy and a massive direct payment to the food producer, one that I support.
Interest rates at the same time have drastically reduced the carrying costs of farm debts through the farm debt review boards that our Government has established and through the Farm Credit Corporation. There have been write-downs on interest rates. There have been programs jointly put into place and jointly agreed to by the various provinces and the Government. All of those things have worked together to reduce substantially the carrying costs of any debt load a farmer might have.
It is not all roses yet. We know we have problems. We know, for example, that there are farmers still losing ground. Their equity base has eroded completely. Many small businesses are in exactly the same position. I have always considered the family farm as a small business. It is treated that way under the tax system and by the producer himself. The lending institutions have always looked at it that way. There is something very special about a food producer. Without him our whole economy deteriorates and falls apart. It has often been said-I forget who said it-you can burn down a city and you can burn down a town, you can destroy the city and you can destroy the town, but like magic, like mushrooms, they will spring up again somewhere else. But if you destroy the farming community, the land and the farms, the cities will wither and die. That is very true and we all know that.
Agri-bond Program
I wonder whether all Members realize that the total federal and provincial Government expenditures for agriculture have today increased to about $4.5 billion annually.
Let me come to agri-bonds. One of the problems with the agri-bond is how to design the instrument in such a way that it will be attractive either to retiring farmers or to the investment community. As a result, it is taking time to study. Members who have worked on this question recognize the real necessity of an agri-bond system which would take some of the burden off the taxpaying public in the programs that we have established. How do we do it is the question. How will the instrument be sold? How will it be presented to the public in general. Those are the questions to be answered and they are under study. I do not think just because we have not brought in an agri-bond, as we indicated we would, that this concept is dead or that we have put it on the back burner. It is not a priority at this time because interest rates have descended from the 22.75 per cent, the very high of five years ago, to the present levels which have become quite manageable. Many producers have interest rates at the 7 per cent level.
I would like to remind Hon. Members that over $5 billion in credit at reduced interest rates has been provided to farmers in financial difficulty through various federal and provincial programs since 1981, primarily programs designed for refinancing. All steps that are taken are taken with the idea that sometime we may come up with an agri-bond that will take some of the burden away from governments. The majority of farmers in financial difficulty are being financed today by federal and provincial credit agencies.
1 am not sure whether the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap whose motion is before us today would accept the idea that federal and provincial credit agencies should do all of the financing. That seems to be the kind of thing that would sit with the philosophy of the New Democratic Party. In my view, the agri-bond itself would be a private instrument, probably marketed through the chartered banks, credit unions or the financial institutions across Canada, or the financial markets, in some way, listed on the stock exchange. One would hope that that kind of instrument could be developed and that is what we are looking at.
I am rather surprised that the Member put this motion before us when $5 billion in credit at reduced interest rates has been provided to farmers in financial difficulty from various federal and provincial agencies. I see that you want me to wind up, Mr. Speaker, and I will. But let me say one thing. Today the majority of farmers in financial difficulty are being financed by federal and provincial credit agencies. I firmly believe that we will develop an agri-bond in due time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to get into this debate primarily because of some of the things the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) stated. I want to respond to them before I deal with the agribond issue. He asked the question, I think, rhetorically, do we support the family farm. Let me tell the Hon. Member that

December 11, 1986
Agri-bond Program
that has been a Conservative policy over the years. I do not have to tell him of the popularity of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) who is known throughout Canada. If he goes into a riding such as min,e where century farms abound-I am sure they do not in other parts of the country-and talked to the farmers there he would find that they remember with tremendous affection the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle- Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who was the Agriculture Minister in the Diefenbaker Government some 25 years ago. He was an example of the feelings all members of this party have towards farmers.
Granted, farmers have had a plethora of problems coming at them from all sides; drought and insects in the west, heavy rains in the east and high fuel prices-you name it, the farmers have been bothered by it recently. However, those problems have all been met by a sympathetic Conservative Government, not with the Salmon Arm salute which the former Prime Minister gave, not with the question, why should we try to sell your wheat. They have been met with real answers; cash where it was possible, credit where it was necessary.
I took last week off and drove by car to Des Moines. That is a long drive at this time of year. I took three young men from my constituency. They are all involved in agriculture in one form or another. We went there to sit in on a conference put on by a firm which publishes a magazine called Successful Farming. The conference was called "Adapt 100". When the ad for this conference was first brought to my attention by a young neighbour, a very aggressive, thoughtful and, I think, successful farmer, we looked at it together and decided we should go down, listen in and see what they were doing. We were astounded. They set out 100 new ideas for farmers, 100 ways that farmers could improve their marketing and production. There were ideas to change methods of production. There were ideas covering all aspects of farm life. What a tremendously encouraging sight it was.
The conference was going to be held in a convention centre in Des Moines. That is not a very big city, about the size of Ottawa. Before they were finished they had to move the opening ceremonies to an arena; over 5,500 people came to that conference just to hear the new ideas. They started at seven o'clock in the morning and went through until nine o'clock at night, thirsty and hungry for new ideas.
Some of the things that came out of this conference were very interesting. One thing I learned was that on average 50 per cent of U.S. farm income last year came from government subsidies. I would like to relate a couple of vignettes from which I got a great chuckle. One chap was expounding about farmers producing corn at $50 a tonne and losing money, whereas Mr. Kellogg sold that corn for $3,600 a tonne and you can bet your life he made money. That same corn was sold for birdseed, together with other grains, at $2,800 a tonne. Once again, everyone made money.
I want to deal a little more pointedly with the motion. The issue of farm finances has been one of this Government's highest priorities. Agri-bonds were proposed as a means of providing farm credit at more favourable interest rates. The Government introduced a number of other measures to this end in its short two years of life. Our initial steps to help farmers included reduced interest rates for those FFC borrowers who were locked into higher rates. The shared risk mortgage program has been dealt with at some length. In addition we expanded the mandate of the FCC appeal boards to provide third party review of farm credit loans under foreclosure. We made farmers effectively free of the federal sales tax on farm fuels and increased the maximum advance under the Advanced Payments for Crops Act.
I know that at least one more of my colleagues wants to speak in this debate so I will move quickly. Others have mentioned, and I will not repeat, the federal Budget which announced farm assistance programs and commodity-based mortgages of which my friend from Algoma was so critical. Farmers in my area seem to find some benefit from that program. Then we have the rural transition program. In addition, assistance continues to be provided to farmers through the Western Grain Stabilization Act, the Agriculture Stabilization Act, crop insurance and dairy and other programs of the federal Government. Direct payments to producers under these programs exceeded an estimated $1.5 billion in 1985.
I will close by saying that our commitment to agriculture was reconfirmed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on October 3 when he indicated in this House that he intended to deliver an additional $1 billion into the hands of Canadian farmers. Just this past week he appeared before the Agriculture Outlook Conference with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and announced details of the plan which you and I and others know has been so well received. We are not embarrassed at all over the fact that the agri-bond program is not yet in place. This Government has done a tremendous job for farmers and will continue to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 must commend the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) for his speech. He touched upon many of the points about which I was anxious to speak. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) insinuated in his remarks that if the Government did not adopt this motion it would show that it did not care about farmers. Nothing could be further from the truth and he knows it. He should not use insinuation to get his point across. However, maybe that is what the job of being in opposition is all about. Nonetheless, I can assure all Members of this House that the actions taken by this Government are on the side of farmers and agricultural production.
In the few remaining moments I have I would like to touch upon what we as a Government have done on agriculture in relation to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. We have been pushing for the inclusion of agriculture in the new round of negotiations. We have been successful because of the
December 11, 1986

efforts of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in making the issue of agricultural subsidies a major point of discussion at the Tokyo Economic Summit last May. The Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board succeeded in bringing together representatives of the world's five major grain exporting nations in Whistler, B.C., to discuss this issue. The Secretary of State for External Affairs led Canada's delegation to Uruguay for the new GATT round. He, in concert with other nations, successively pushed for inclusion of this item in the GATT round. That is just another example of how this Government is concerned about the welfare of farmers and about what happens in agriculture.
In conclusion, our action plan for agriculture is very clear. The Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings referred to the $1 billion pay-out this week. I can say that we will continue to represent the interests of farmers at the international level and of course here in Canada.

subtopic: AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT-REVIEW OF PRIVATE PENSION PLANS
AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT-REVIEW OF PRIVATE PENSION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that you had the benefit of knowing my late father. That is most unfortunate because I know you would have liked him very much. My late father was a man who our friends and colleagues in the New Democratic Party would have described as an ordinary Canadian. To me he was a very extraordinary Canadian, just like your own father, Mr. Speaker, just like millions of other Canadians across this land.
One thing that was dominant in my father's life was his pension plan. His pension plan was extremely important to him and played a major role in all the decisions he made throughout his adult life. That was understandable. I know you will understand that when I tell you that my father worked for one company for more than 40 years. He went through the Great Depression, as did so many others. He knew what it was to work, he knew what it was to be out of work, and he knew what it was to have the fear of a lack of financial security. That fact was a great influence in his life. Financial security and his pension were always important to him because he had lived through the Depression.
Adjournment Debate
In addition, he lived through the Second World War. He knew the problems of financial security and the lack of financial security which resulted from the Second World War. He knew the problems of widows and children who had no breadwinner in the family and had no financial security.
Throughout his entire adult life he worked with people from similar backgrounds, people who had the same concerns and experiences, people who knew the problems of a lack of financial security. He knew as well of the financial security, concerns and problems of single women because he supervised a great number of women. At that time the women in the workforce were mainly single women. Women were and still are underpaid and still lack adequate pension plans. It was most important to them to have at least a modest form of pension plan. That financial security was an essential cornerstone of their existence. My father knew as well of run-away inflation which ate into savings and pension plans and turned them into a very modest sum compared to the work done to save for retirement.
In addition, he knew the background of his ancestors, his father, his grandfather and his great grandfather. In the history of our family people have died in abject poverty because there were no pension plans, there was no security. It was through the combination of all these influences on my own father's life and, through him, on my own life, that I understand, just as he did, how important pension plans were and are and what a major role and priority pensions play in the lives of so many people.
I know your father, Mr. Speaker, would feel devastated, as my father would, if suddenly his pension plan collapsed or failed. That is something on which you and I, Sir, as guardians of federal pension plans, must keep a very close eye. I am concerned, and I am sure you are as well, Mr. Speaker, that two banks have gone under just in the last short while. That is why, again, it is so important that all pension plans under federal supervision be properly looked after and policed.
The Auditor General has given us a warning that there is some problem and we have to be on our guard that perhaps these pension plans are not being adequately policed. Therefore, we have to ask ourselves, for instance, about the lack of on-site inspections, the question of proper appraisals, investments, real estate or mortgages, about loan concentration problems and why 16 financial institutions under federal control and supervision have failed since 1980. Those are all questions we must be concerned about. I know you are just as concerned, Mr. Speaker, as myself.
We are happy that our own Department of Insurance is coming out with a new Pension Benefits Standards Act as of the first of the year. We are happy that all of the ways of looking after these things are being reviewed, but at the same time we want to make sure they do an even better job than they have been doing. I hope tonight we will receive assurances from the Parliamentary Secretary that those pension plans of

December 11, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Canadian senior citizens which are supervised by the federal Government will be adequately protected not only for today but for years and years to come.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT-REVIEW OF PRIVATE PENSION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answering the question and comments by my hon. colleague, I would first like to stress that those plans mentioned by my colleague, the pension plans, are examined when they are tabled. Secondly, they are reviewed at least every three years or at even shorter intervals. Such examinations involve ascertaining that those plans meet legal requirements, assessing actuarial liabilities and reviewing the assets of those pension plans to make sure that they are properly run.
The report of the Auditor General actually refers to another inspection program, an on-site inspection program as opposed to the review program I just mentioned. Admittedly, on-site inspections are not carried out by the Department of Insurance in the case of every plan. But the program has been giving very satisfactory results to date, and there have obviously been fewer on-site inspections than for the rest.
The Auditor General clearly raised a number of questions dealing with the inspection practices of the Department of Insurance with respect to the supervision of pension plans. At that stage, the Department of Insurance, as you know, Mr. Speaker, initiated a study to get the facts and verify the allegations of the Auditor General.
That study would include a detailed cost-benefit analysis of increased supervision, based on the fact that most of the cost of that increased supervision will be assumed by the pension plans themselves in the form of registration fees required by the law.
We know, Mr. Speaker, and no doubt my hon. colleague knows that 95 per cent of the contributors of those pension plans under federal control contribute to specific benefit systems. If the investment performance of the plan does not meet the actuarial projections, the employer has an obligation to complement the assets portfolio so that adequate provision is made for the payment of benefits.
I therefore think that this should alleviate the concerns raised in the remarks of my hon. colleague. He also knows that the Government is presently drafting changes in the federal pension plans legislation.
A number of changes have already been introduced and will result in improved survivors' benefits, pension transferability as well as a faster devolution of pension rights.
These explanations, Mr. Speaker, should take care of all the concerns expressed by my hon. colleague.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO REINSTATE DEMOCRATIC SYSTEM IN KANASETAKE INDIAN BAND
INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO REINSTATE DEMOCRATIC SYSTEM IN KANASETAKE INDIAN BAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 30 I put a question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) about a particular problem at the Kanasetake Reserve in Oka. The reserve is now referred to as Kanasetake. Before, it was Oka, and I say this for the benefit of those who might not have been aware of the change.
Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister whether he had the authority to intervene in matters concerning the manner in which the band's chief and council members are elected and how they administer the band.
The Minister replied that he did not intervene or interfere with the elections or customs of the Indian government of the Oka band.
Mr. Speaker, what happens when there are two factions with totally different positions and there is a tie? Who decides? Does the Minister intervene to "split the band" or does he try and find out what the problem is with the system?
Mr. Speaker, I have here a submission that was presented to me by representatives of the Kanasetake Indian League for Democracy, which says: That in 1979, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development had recognized a hereditary system according to the Custom & Hereditary Chief formula, with 81 people who raised their hands in the hall, although there were 270 members who were eligible to vote present. That is what that this group had to say.
The band council, elected according to the hereditary system, says that they were duly elected according to the system they had always had, and that after elections were held in 1971 and 1979, the Indians who were against the system went to court. There were a number of problems with provincial court that heard the case, and later, they said: No, this is a federal matter, and so forth. On November 12, the same clan mothers decided to unseat the big chief they had elected, and the band members who were not aware of this-there might be a communications problem-but they were not aware of this at all, and, Mr. Speaker, as I explained earlier, they came to see me and asked me to intervene. I will read the last paragraph of the letter which says, in English, and I quote:
On behalf of the Oka Band Members who have signed this petition, I will appreciate this matter being addressed to the House of Commons without undue delay, from the viewpoint of acquiring government recognition of the fact that the people of Oka, no longer, cannot nor will not tolerate a dictatorship and are in desperate need of government assistance to entrench the democratic process once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, I was told 230 members of the Kanasetake Band had signed the petition, out of 537 registered members. The petition reads as follows:
December 11, 1986

"We, the undersigned, members of the Kanasetake Reserve, would like to select candidates for the big chiefs position and for other chief positions that will be available in the future. We also want to be able to have a say in the final selection and also in the term of the chiefs mandate".
Mr. Speaker, it seems important to me that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) should be involved in an issue as basic as democracy when a dispute seriously divides a community plagued with economic conditions of a most prejudicial nature because many of its members live on welfare and there are no jobs. The Kanasetake Band does not live on a reservation as defined by the Indian Act. This is rather a federal land. This fact has given rise to various problems because they would like to be recognized and have their own territory.
Recently a decision was made and their land claim is now completed.
Now I would like the Minister to tell us what he intends to do about solving once and for all the problem raised by the Kanasetake Band's election system and since a new chief has just been elected it would perhaps be possible and I am looking forward to a reply from the Parliamentary Secretary on this matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTERVENE TO REINSTATE DEMOCRATIC SYSTEM IN KANASETAKE INDIAN BAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) has raised a question about the Kanesatake Band system of local government and more specifically the method of selecting the chief and council. The present system of government, which is sometimes referred to as the life chiefs system, is rooted in the customs and traditions of the Iroquois confederacy and is viewed by many band members as a vital link with the Mohawk cultural tradition and a guarantee that the future maintenance of Mohawk identity will continue.
The band members opposed to the traditional chiefs' system are of the opinion that such a system is elitist and that it perpetrates the domination of the band membership by a few individuals. It should be noted, however, that the current system was adopted voluntarily by the majority of the band membership in 1969. Therefore, the solution for which the Hon. Member is looking lies within that system. It is the right and prerogative of the band members to amend or reject the current system by an additional majority vote.
As has been stated in the House, it is inappropriate for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) to interfere in any of the band affairs or to attempt to alter unilaterally its elective system. With respect to the Kanesatake Band there is also a compelling legal reason restricting ministerial action on the band's elective system. The lands occupied by the Kanesatake Band known as the Oka Reserve were purchased by the federal Government in 1945 for use by the band. However, strictly speaking the lands are federal Crown lands, not reserve lands, although they are
Adjournment Debate
commonly referred to as such. Therefore, the election provisions in the Indian Act, which apply only to reserve lands, cannot be invoked in this case.
As mentioned earlier, not only would a ministerial intervention be inappropriate, but the Minister is not in a legal position to take direct action to solve these difficulties. Officials are prepared to continue to work with the various factions in the band to seek a solution. The Minister is sympathetic to the difficult situation faced by the band, and would like to see a successful and early resolution of the problem. However, it must be recognized that the initiative to change is essentially in the hands of the band membership itself.

Mr. Speaker, on June 26, 1986, the then Minister of Communications tabled legislation in the House which would require that federal and provincial government departments, agencies and municipalities, pay radio station licence fees on the same basis as private users. The consequences of this measure were not immediately apparent, but in due course they became known.
The many volunteer fire departments throughout Canada were included with those organizations which were going to be required to foot the bill for these changes. It was my feeling that those volunteer agencies could not afford this, and it should not be required.
In the course of the next few weeks, while continuing to receive more and more requests from unhappy volunteers, I made representations to the Hon. Minister on behalf of my constituents, and indeed all of Canada's volunteer firemen. Local fire departments and municipalities began a concerted effort to convince the Department of Communications that this measure was neither beneficial nor cost effective for our many volunteer fire departments.
Many of them passed resolutions such as the following:
WHEREAS fast, dependable communications are necesssary for municipal police, fire and public works departments and are demanded by the public they serve;
AND WHEREAS two-way radio plays a vital role in the communication network of most Nova Scotia municipal units;
AND WHEREAS a news release dated June 26, 1986 from the office of the Minister of Communications (distributed to N.S. municipal units by the Halifax office of DOC on September 9, 1986) stated that starting April 1, 1987 municipalities, along with provincial government departments, will pay radiolicence fees on the same basis as private users;
AND WHEREAS this will result in a 400 per cent annual increase to the cost of obtaining radio licenses;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Union of Nova Scotia Municipalities requests the Government of Nova Scotia to do everything possible to attempt to have the Department of Communications reverse their policy of license fee increases;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Union of Nova Scotia Municipalities forward its concern over this unfair cost increase to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities for support at the national level.

December 11, 1986
Adjournment Debate
The small municipalities and the volunteer fire deparments are the focal points for many of our rural communities. These dedicated citizens who devote so much of their time to public service certainly deserve and indeed have been assured of this Government's support and encouragement.
In the Throne Speech we promised further support to encourage the growth of volunteerism in our society. The proposed increases in radio licence fees would have averaged 400 per cent in Nova Scotia. I received 18 written submissions from volunteer fire departments within my riding seeking my co-operation and assistance in opposing these increases.
At the conclusion of the many strong representations made to the Hon. Minister in the House last Monday, I asked whether or not she had been able to resolve this matter. I was very pleased to hear her response, which I shall read:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for South West Nova for his representations on this issue. Indeed, I have received representations on the issue from a number of other Members.
I should like to advise him and the House that I have decided to defer for the time being any changes to the regulations as they apply to radio licence fees for municipalities and volunteer fire departments.
I should like to commend the Hon. Minister and the Department of Communications for accepting the recommendations made on the matter. Indeed it is gratifying that the outstanding efforts of many volunteer firemen have been acknowledged in this way.
Since the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Mailly) is present in the Chamber this evening, I ask her to make a few comments on the subject.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Claudy Mailly (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the question of my colleague. As the Minister said in response to his question of December 1, she gave serious consideration to his representations and concluded that she would not change anything to the preferential treatment now given to municipalities, therefore to volunteer fire departments in the communities represented by the Hon. Member and in other localities throughout Canada.
The Hon. Member had asked the Minister whether she would be prepared to refrain from taking regulatory measures likely to increase municipal radio licence fees. If I understand correctly, the Hon. Member's question specifically related to volunteer firemen, and his concern was due to the existence of the Bill which had been introduced in June and to which my colleague was referring.
First I should like to point out that Bill C-3 which will probably come up for second reading tomorrow and which has already been studied by the Senate has nothing to do with regulations governing municipalities and volunteer fire departments. Therefore he should not worry. This Bill has nothing to do with municipal preferential treatment. It is simply a matter of making the provinces and federal Government departments pay their share of radio licence fees. Until now, Mr. Speaker, both these groups had been exempted and Bill C-3 concerns them, not the municipalities.
The Minister will be holding consultations precisely to decide just how municipalities should fare with respect to the cost recovery operation mentioned by the Minister of Finance in November 1984. Clearly the Minister does not want to create problems for smaller municipalities and she understands quite well the importance of volunteer fire departments as well as the services they provide to thousands of small municipalities throughout Canada. Therefore, she will show the greatest responsibility and compassion before deciding what to do regulation-wise concerning municipalities. But it is not for today and it has nothing to do with Bill C-3. I should like to assure my honourable colleague that the Minister has duly received his representations and indeed, she has personally congratulated him for the effort he is making on behalf of his constituents.
